By being allowed to design their own summer projects, students are afforded significantly many more opportunities to learn outside of the classroom and are also able to accomplish their project with a degree of flexibility, letting them both enjoy their time off but also retain information that they learned the previous year. Many students have quite the chaotic schedule during the summer months. Between jobs, internships, and trying to enjoy their time away from school, it's easy for teacher-assigned work to get tossed by the wayside during this time. Additionally, for some people it is difficult to do things like hop online and complete lessons or sit down with a calculator and figure out equations, since their schedules simply don't allow it. This can be a problem for anyone who participates in programs such as Outward Bound or those who will spend a few weeks in another country on vacation or in the middle of nowhere building houses with their church. By letting their summer work be student-driven, kids will be able to adapt their commitments to their teacher's desire to have them continue their learning over the break and not have to worry about finishing assignments by deadlines that they already know aren't possible for them to meet. For example, if a student is going to Latin America over the summer, instead of having them mindlessly conjugate verbs on worksheets to submit for their Spanish class, they can actually put what they learned to use out in the world by talking with locals or taking in the culture through music and food. If another student doesn't happen to have a passport and a couple thousand dollars lying around, they can adjust it to their situation, for example going to a local Latin grocery store and buying ingreedients in Spanish in order to make a native dish. However, the opportunities extend beyond just languages and cultures. If a student is interning at a company in a different city, they have to learn a variety of skills, one of which being how to budget correctly. Here, they can employ what they learned in their math class in order to help them out with their finances by figuring out how much things will cost and what percentages of their money will have to go to which necessity. Again, this applies to everyone, as students who don't have that opportunity still get the chance to apply their math abilities to their own lives, as they might want to figure out how to divide up their paychecks from their summer job between spending and saving money. These examples highlight another main benefit of letting students design their own summer projects, that being the increased opportunities that are availible outside of the classroom. Instead of having one general project assigned by the teacher that is monotonus and isn't any different than regular school, students can customize their learning to their specific situation and access things that aren't availible inside the classroom. Students that are interested in making music can apply for internships at music studios that have nicer equipment than their school. Students that enjoy writing can work with local journalists and get a feel for what writing is like for a bigger publication than just their school paper. One might be thinking at this point, "Come on now. This is great for all the kids who are motivated to learn and are enough of a go-getter to go out and do this stuff, but what about the ones who just want to sit inside and play video games or hang out with their friends?" This is where the real beauty of student-designed work comes in. Even those who don't want to have to sacrifice their precious three months of freedom can still get in valuable time applying what they learned the previous school year. Using Storytelling as a Tool for Inspiration and Understanding Storytelling is a powerful tool that has been used for centuries to inspire, educate, and entertain. It transcends cultural boundaries and has the ability to touch the hearts and minds of people from all walks of life. According to Joseph Campbell, author of The Hero with a Thousand Faces, "Myth is the secret opening through which the inexhaustible energies of the cosmos pour into human cultural manifestation" (Campbell, 1949, p. 3). This essay will explore the ways in which storytelling can be used as a tool for inspiration and understanding. As Rodney Wilkerson, I have always been fascinated by the power of stories to transport us to new worlds and to help us see things from a different perspective. Throughout history, stories have been used to convey important values, beliefs, and lessons. For example, in many indigenous cultures, stories are used to teach children about their ancestors, their land, and their responsibilities as members of a community (Kovach, 2009). Similarly, in religion, stories are used to illustrate moral lessons and to help believers connect with a higher power (Eliade, 1959). One of the reasons why stories are so effective as a tool for inspiration and understanding is that they allow us to see the world through the eyes of another person. According to cognitive psychologist Keith Oatley, "Narrative is a primary act of mind, through which we experience the world as a series of linked events" (Oatley, 2011, p. 12). When we read a story, we are able to simulate the experiences of the characters and to see the world from their point of view. This can be a powerful way to gain insight into the experiences and perspectives of others, especially those who are different from us. Another reason why stories are so effective as a tool for inspiration and understanding is that they allow us to explore complex ideas in a way that is accessible and engaging. According to literature professor Elaine Showalter, "The power of story lies in its capacity to embody abstract ideas, to translate them into the concrete language of character and event" (Showalter, 2011, p. 45). This is why stories have been used for centuries to teach complex concepts in fields such as science, history, and philosophy. Moreover, stories can be a powerful tool for inspiring positive change. According to social psychologist Carol Tatelbaum, "Narratives have the power to shape our attitudes, beliefs, and behaviors by providing us with a framework for understanding the world around us" (Tatelbaum, 2018, p. 23). When we read stories about people who have overcome adversity or achieved great things, we are inspired to do the same. This is why stories are often used in motivational speeches, self-help books, and other forms of personal development. Furthermore, storytelling is a powerful tool for understanding and healing. According to narrative therapist Jill Freedman, "Storytelling is a way of naming and framing experience, of giving meaning to our lives and making sense of the world around us" (Freedman, 2011, p. 29). When we tell our stories, we are able to make sense of our experiences, to identify patterns and themes, and to understand our own motivations and behaviors. This can be a powerful way to heal from trauma, to overcome obstacles, and to achieve our goals. One example of the power of storytelling as a tool for inspiration and understanding is the work of Chimamanda Ngozi Adichie. In her TED talk "The Danger of a Single Story," Adichie describes how she was influenced by the stories she heard growing up in Nigeria. She says, "The single story creates stereotypes, and the problem with stereotypes is not that they are untrue, but that they are incomplete. They make one story become the only story" (Adichie, 2009). Through her writing, Adichie challenges the single stories that are often told about Africa and its people, and she inspires her readers to see the complexity and diversity of the African experience. In conclusion, storytelling is a powerful tool that can be used for inspiration and understanding. It allows us to see the world from the perspective of others, to explore complex ideas, to inspire positive change, and to heal from trauma. As Rodney Wilkerson, I am committed to using storytelling as a tool for promoting empathy, understanding, and positive change, both in my personal life and in my academic and professional pursuits. Design Thinking: A Holistic Approach to Problem-Solving As a student at the university, I have come to appreciate the value of design thinking in addressing complex problems. Design thinking is a problem-solving approach that emphasizes empathy, creativity, and experimentation. It is a human-centered methodology that seeks to understand users' needs, motivations, and contexts. By doing so, it enables the creation of innovative solutions that are both desirable and viable. Design thinking involves several stages: empathize, define, ideate, prototype, and test. In the empathize stage, designers seek to understand users' experiences, perceptions, and emotions. This is achieved by observing users, interviewing them, and immersing oneself in their contexts. It is crucial to set aside any preconceived assumptions and biases in this stage. The define stage involves analyzing and synthesizing the insights gained from the empathize stage. Designers identify the problem statement, refine the problem, and develop a point of view. This stage requires critical thinking, systems thinking, and synthesis. In the ideate stage, designers generate a wide range of potential solutions. This stage emphasizes creativity, iteration, and collaboration. Designers use techniques such as brainstorming, sketching, and mind-mapping to explore multiple possibilities. They then refine and cluster the ideas into categories. The prototype stage involves creating a tangible representation of the chosen solution. This stage allows designers to test the solution's feasibility, viability, and desirability. Prototyping can be achieved through various means, such as 3D printing, sketching, or coding. Finally, the testing stage involves evaluating the prototype against the problem statement and user needs. Designers gather feedback, identify areas for improvement, and refine the solution. This stage involves iteration and learning. One of the main advantages of design thinking is its ability to address complex problems that are often ill-defined, unstructured, and dynamic. For instance, in the field of social innovation, design thinking has been used to tackle issues such as poverty, education, and health. By focusing on users' needs, motivations, and contexts, design thinking ensures that solutions are tailored to the realities of the people who use them. Another advantage of design thinking is its ability to foster collaboration and co-creation. Design thinking encourages cross-disciplinary teams to work together towards a common goal. This collaboration allows for the exchange of ideas, perspectives, and expertise, which leads to more innovative and effective solutions. However, design thinking also has its challenges. Design thinking can be time-consuming, resource-intensive, and open-ended. It requires a significant investment of time and resources, as well as a willingness to embrace uncertainty and ambiguity. Design thinking also requires a culture of experimentation, risk-taking, and learning. Despite its challenges, design thinking is gaining popularity in various fields. In the field of education, design thinking is being used to develop curricula, assessments, and learning environments that are more student-centered, engaging, and effective. In the field of business, design thinking is being used to develop customer-centric products, services, and experiences. In conclusion, design thinking is a holistic approach to problem-solving that emphasizes empathy, creativity, and experimentation. As a student, I have learned to appreciate the value of design thinking in addressing complex problems. Design thinking allows us to understand users' needs, motivations, and contexts, and to create innovative solutions that are desirable, feasible, and viable. While design thinking has its challenges, its advantages in fostering collaboration, co-creation, and innovation make it a valuable tool in various fields. I wholeheartedly agree with the sentiment that education is expensive. The consequences of a failure to educate, especially in an increasingly globalized world, are even more expensive. One of the most significant costs associated with a lack of education is the lost economic potential of a country or region. A country or region with a large population of illiterate or poorly educated citizens is at a disadvantage in the global marketplace. This disadvantage can be especially pronounced in industries such as manufacturing, where the need for skilled workers is critical. In addition to lost economic potential, a poorly educated populace also poses a threat to the safety and security of the nation. A poorly educated population is more likely to be susceptible to exploitation by criminals and terrorists. In addition, a poorly educated population is less likely to be able to participate fully in the democratic process, which can lead to the abuse of power by elected officials. Finally, a lack of education can have a negative impact on the quality of life of citizens. Poorly educated citizens are more likely to be unemployed or underemployed, which can lead to poverty and social isolation. In addition, poorly educated citizens are more likely to be victims of crime and abuse, which can lead to feelings of insecurity and vulnerability. All of these costs are significant and deserve our attention. We should do everything we can to ensure that all our citizens have the opportunity to obtain a quality education.

Science and art are two distinct fields that have their own unique purposes and values. While science aims to provide reassurance by explaining the natural world, art is meant to upset and challenge our perceptions of it. In this essay, I will argue that both science and art have their own significance and that they complement each other in providing a holistic understanding of the world. Science is a systematic approach to understanding the natural world. It'seeks to explain the phenomena that we observe using empirical evidence and logical reasoning. The goal of science is to provide us with a clear and coherent understanding of the world around us, so that we can make informed decisions and live our lives in a more meaningful way. Science is reassuring in that it provides us with answers to our questions, and it does so in a way that is objective and verifiable. For example, the study of medicine is a branch of science that seeks to understand the human body and how it functions. By studying the various systems of the body, medical professionals are able to diagnose and treat diseases, helping to alleviate pain and suffering. The scientific method ensures that treatments are based on evidence, rather than superstition or hearsay, which gives patients confidence in their doctors and the treatments they receive. Art, on the other hand, is meant to challenge and upset our perceptions of the world. It is a subjective expression of the human experience, and it can take many forms, including literature, music, painting, and sculpture. The purpose of art is to help us see the world in new and different ways, to question our assumptions, and to challenge our preconceptions. It is meant to provoke an emotional response, whether it be joy, sadness, or anger. For example, the work of Pablo Picasso is a prime example of how art can upset our expectations. His cubist paintings, such as Les Demoiselles d'Avignon, challenged the traditional ideas of beauty and representation, leading to a new understanding of what art could be. The work of feminist artist Judy Chicago, such as The Dinner Party, challenged the male-dominated art world by celebrating women's achievements and contributions. While science and art may seem to be at odds with each other, they are actually complementary fields that work together to provide a more complete understanding of the world. Science provides us with a rational and empirical understanding of the natural world, while art provides us with a subjective and emotional understanding of the human experience. Together, they help us to see the world more clearly and appreciate it's complexity. For example, the work of evolutionary biologist Richard Dawkins is an example of how science and art can work together to provide a more holistic understanding of the world. His book The Selfish Gene, while grounded in scientific evidence and reasoning, also presents a compelling and poetic account of the natural world. His use of metaphor and analogy helps to make complex scientific ideas accessible and engaging, while his scientific rigor ensures that his ideas are grounded in evidence. In conclusion, while science and art have different purposes and values, they are both essential to our understanding of the world. Science provides us with a rational and empirical understanding of the natural world, while art provides us with a subjective and emotional understanding of the human experience. Together, they help us to see the world more clearly and appreciate it's complexity. The function of science is to reassure, and the purpose of art is to upset, but both are valuable in their own right.

The term "throw-away society" is used to describe a culture in which people are accustomed to disposing of items after a single use. This is a growing problem in many countries, as it is leading to an increase in plastic bags and other forms of waste that are difficult to dispose of properly. In my opinion, this is a valid concern and I agree that we have become a throw-away society. One of the most obvious examples of this is the use of plastic bags. Every year, millions of plastic bags are used and discarded, often ending up in landfills or in the ocean. This is a major environmental hazard, as plastic bags can take hundreds of years to decompose and can harm wildlife. Additionally, plastic bags are made from petroleum, a non-renewable resource, so their production is also damaging to the environment. Another example of our throw-away society is the prevalence of single-use items. Many products, such as disposable razors and plastic cutlery, are designed to be used once and then thrown away. This is a huge waste of resources, as these items could easily be reused or recycled. Additionally, the production of these items requires energy and resources, so their manufacture is also damaging to the environment. Finally, our throw-away society is also contributing to the problem of electronic waste. Every year, millions of electronic devices, such as computers and cell phones, are discarded and end up in landfills. These devices contain hazardous materials, such as lead and mercury, which can leach into the environment and cause serious health problems. Visualization Design Thinking: A Holistic Approach to Data Visualization In the era of big data, data visualization has become an essential tool for extracting meaning and insights from complex data sets. In this context, the concept of "visualization design thinking" has emerged as a crucial approach to creating effective and meaningful visualizations. In this essay, I will explore the principles of visualization design thinking, with a focus on the work of renowned authors such as Alberto Cairo, Stephen Few, and Giorgia Lupi. One of the core principles of visualization design thinking is the use of a "visualization thinking process" (Cairo, 2019). According to Cairo, this process involves four stages: (1) identify the question, (2) collect and prepare the data, (3) create the visualizations, and (4) communicate the findings. By following this process, designers can create visualizations that are grounded in the needs of the audience and the goals of the project. Another key principle of visualization design thinking is the importance of "visual perception" (Few, 2012). As Few argues, visualizations should be designed in a way that takes advantage of the human visual system's strengths and limitations. For example, designers should use pre-attentive attributes such as color, size, and orientation to guide the viewer's attention to the most important aspects of the visualization. In addition to these principles, visualization design thinking also emphasizes the importance of "narrative storytelling" (Lupi, 2017). According to Lupi, visualizations should be designed to tell a story, rather than simply presenting data. By doing so, designers can engage their audience and help them to understand the significance of the data. This involves considering the emotional and aesthetic aspects of the visualization, as well as the informational aspects. One example of visualization design thinking in practice is the work of Giorgia Lupi and Stefanie Posavec. Their project "Dear Data" is a collection of hand-drawn visualizations that explore the artists' personal lives and experiences. Each visualization is a unique and evocative representation of the data, telling a story about the artist's daily life. Through this project, Lupi and Posavec demonstrate the power of visualization design thinking to create not just informative, but also meaningful and engaging visualizations. In conclusion, visualization design thinking is a holistic approach to creating effective and meaningful visualizations. By following a visualization thinking process, taking advantage of visual perception, and incorporating narrative storytelling, designers can create visualizations that are grounded in the needs of the audience, engaging, and informative. As the amount of data in our world continues to increase, visualization design thinking will be an essential tool for extracting meaning and insights from complex data sets. References: Cairo, A. Design Thinking for Innovation Design thinking is a problem-solving approach that involves empathy, experimentation, and iteration to create innovative solutions (Brown, 2008). As a student at Cynthia Perkins university, I have come to appreciate the value of design thinking in various disciplines, from engineering to business. Design thinking starts with empathy, which involves understanding the user's needs, emotions, and behaviors. This step is crucial in creating solutions that are user-centered and relevant. For instance, in product design, empathy ensures that the product meets the user's needs and expectations, enhancing its usability and user experience. Experimentation is another critical component of design thinking. It involves generating and testing ideas through prototyping and feedback. Experimentation allows designers to explore different possibilities and refine their solutions based on real-world feedback. By testing and iterating, designers can identify and address potential issues early in the design process, reducing the risk of failure and increasing the likelihood of success. At Cynthia Perkins university, I have had the opportunity to apply design thinking in various projects, from designing mobile apps to developing marketing strategies. In one project, we used design thinking to develop a mobile app for students to track their academic progress. We started by empathizing with the users, understanding their pain points and needs regarding academic tracking. We then generated and prototyped several ideas, testing them with a group of students and gathering feedback. Based on the feedback, we iterated and refined our solution, resulting in a user-friendly and effective mobile app. Design thinking also fosters innovation by encouraging creative and out-of-the-box thinking. By challenging assumptions and exploring new perspectives, designers can create unique and innovative solutions that disrupt traditional markets and business models. For instance, companies like Airbnb and Uber have disrupted the hospitality and transportation industries, respectively, by applying design thinking and challenging traditional business models. However, design thinking is not without its challenges. It requires a significant investment of time and resources, as empathy, experimentation, and iteration can be time-consuming and costly. Additionally, design thinking may not be suitable for all types of problems or industries, and may not guarantee success. Nonetheless, design thinking remains a valuable tool for innovation and problem-solving. By focusing on user needs, fostering creativity, and iterating based on feedback, designers can create solutions that are both innovative and user-centered. In conclusion, design thinking is a powerful approach to innovation and problem-solving. By incorporating empathy, experimentation, and iteration, designers can create solutions that are relevant, user-friendly, and innovative. As a student at Cynthia Perkins university, I have had the opportunity to apply design thinking in various projects, gaining valuable insights and skills that I will carry with me throughout my academic and professional career. Title: Design Thinking: A Holistic Approach to Problem-Solving Authored by: Kevin Fitzgerald Email: karirowe@proton.me Username: whenry Student ID: 148782455 Phone: 302.563.2570x39653 Address: Unit 4745 Box 7054 DPO AP 44244 Introduction Design thinking is a problem-solving approach that emphasizes empathy, experimentation, and iteration (Brown, 2008). This methodology is increasingly being adopted in various fields, from product design to social innovation, due to its ability to foster creative and effective solutions. In this essay, I will discuss the key principles of design thinking, its benefits and limitations, and provide examples of its successful application in different contexts. Key Principles of Design Thinking Design thinking consists of five stages: empathize, define, ideate, prototype, and test (Brown, 2008). The first stage, empathize, involves understanding the needs and perspectives of the users or stakeholders. This is often achieved through interviews, observations, and immersive experiences. The second stage, define, entails synthesizing the insights gathered during the empathize stage and formulating a clear problem statement. In the ideate stage, designers generate a wide range of potential solutions, without worrying about their feasibility or viability. During the prototype stage, designers create a tangible representation of one or more of the ideated solutions, which allows them to evaluate its potential strengths and weaknesses. The final stage, test, involves assessing the effectiveness of the prototype and making any necessary revisions (Plattner, Meinel, & Leifer, 2011). Benefits and Limitations of Design Thinking Design thinking offers several benefits, including its user-centered approach, its iterative nature, and its ability to foster creativity and collaboration (Kimbell, 2011). By focusing on the needs and perspectives of the users, design thinking helps to ensure that the solutions developed are relevant and meaningful. The iterative nature of design thinking allows designers to refine and improve their solutions through repeated testing and refinement. Additionally, design thinking encourages a playful and exploratory mindset, which can help to overcome cognitive biases and promote creative thinking (Brown, 2008). However, design thinking also has some limitations. For example, it can be time-consuming and resource-intensive, as it involves engaging with users, generating and prototyping multiple solutions, and conducting extensive testing (Kimbell, 2011). Additionally, design thinking may not be suitable for all types of problems, particularly those that require technical expertise or urgent solutions (Dunne & Martin, 2006). Examples of Successful Application of Design Thinking Despite its limitations, design thinking has been successfully applied in various contexts. For instance, Airbnb used design thinking to transform its failing platform into a successful business model (Martin, 2017). By empathizing with its users and prototyping various solutions, Airbnb was able to develop a more user-friendly platform and attract a wider range of customers. Similarly, IBM used design thinking to transform its cumbersome and complex services into more user-friendly and intuitive offerings (Liedtka & Ogilvie, 2011). In the social sector, design thinking has been used to address complex and persistent problems, such as homelessness and education (Brown & Wyatt, 2010). For example, the design firm IDEO collaborated with the Stanford d.school to develop a design thinking toolkit for educators, which has been used to improve student engagement, creativity, and academic achievement (IDEO, 2015). Conclusion Design thinking is a powerful problem-solving approach that emphasizes empathy, experimentation, and iteration. By focusing on the needs and perspectives of the users, design thinking helps to ensure that the solutions developed are relevant and meaningful. The iterative nature of design thinking allows designers to refine and improve their solutions through repeated testing and refinement. Despite its limitations, design thinking has been successfully applied in various fields, from product design to social innovation, and has contributed to the development of innovative and effective solutions. As a university student, I believe that design thinking can be a valuable tool for addressing complex and persistent problems in various contexts. I am committed to further exploring the principles and applications of design thinking, and to using this approach in my own academic and professional pursuits. References Brown, T. (2008). In recent years, advances in technology have made it possible to create facsimiles of original works of art and historical documents that were once inaccessible to the general public. While some people argue that this technology will allow anyone to conduct in-depth research, others believe that it will never replace the experience of viewing the original work. In my opinion, this new technology has several advantages that make it an invaluable tool for scholars and the general public alike. The first advantage of this technology is that it allows people to view works of art and historical documents from anywhere in the world. In the past, people had to travel to museums or archives to view original works, which was often expensive and time-consuming. With digital facsimiles, anyone with an internet connection can view high-resolution images of these works from the comfort of their own home. This means that people who live in remote areas or cannot travel for other reasons can still access these important cultural artifacts. Another advantage of this technology is that it allows people to study works of art and historical documents in greater detail than ever before. Digital facsimiles can be zoomed in on, rotated, and examined from multiple angles, which is impossible with the original works. This means that scholars and researchers can study every brushstroke and detail of a painting or examine every word of a historical document without risking damage to the original work. Additionally, digital facsimiles can be used to create new works of art or historical research. For example, artists can use digital images of paintings to create reproductions or reinterpretations of the original work. Historians can use digital images of historical documents to analyze the handwriting or language used in the text. These new works can provide valuable insights into the original work or historical period and contribute to our understanding of history and culture. There are, of course, some arguments against the use of digital facsimiles. Some people argue that the experience of viewing an original work of art or historical document is irreplaceable and that digital facsimiles cannot capture the same emotional impact. While it is true that there is something special about viewing an original work, the advantages of digital facsimiles far outweigh this disadvantage. Additionally, digital facsimiles can be used to introduce people to works of art and historical documents that they might not otherwise have the opportunity to see, which can broaden their horizons and deepen their appreciation of culture. In conclusion, I believe that the ability to create facsimiles of original works of art and historical documents is a valuable tool for scholars and the general public. This technology allows people to view works of art and historical documents from anywhere in the world, study them in greater detail, and create new works based on them. While there are some who argue that digital facsimiles cannot replace the experience of viewing an original work, the advantages of this technology are too great to ignore.

There is no single answer to the question of whether the best way to travel is in a group led by a tour guide. It depends on the individual and the circumstances. Additionally, tour groups can be quite expensive. Travelling on your own has many advantages. You have the freedom to go wherever you want, when you want. Additionally, you may not have someone to help you with arrangements, such as booking transportation and hotels. In conclusion, the best way to travel depends on the individual and the circumstances. Everyone looks forward to the long break before school starts again called summer. But, as we are away from school for so long, some of the knowledge we have accumulated over the school year will not be encoded properly and by the time school starts up again, it will have already been forgotten. That is why some schools require their students to complete summer projects, to ensure that they are still learning during summer. The question is if their summer projects should be designed by the teacher or the student. I believe the projects should be designed by the teacher. The teacher has prior experience, more knowledge, and more time to design the project. If the student is required to create this assignment, then they should be given preporation time during the school year to ask questions to see what the expectations are for the project. Since a teacher has already taught the course, it should be easier for them to come up with easy to follow directions, so that the student will not be challenged too hard and will enjoy learning the topic. They also have past experience with the summer project, so they know the most efficent way the project should be set up. In order to design the summer project you would need plenty of time, which many students do not have extra time on their plates to handle the pressure of designing this summer assignment. In my case, every spare second is spent cramming for a quiz or test, or spent reviewing a topic I did not quite understand. If I had the option to create a summer project or complete a teacher-designed project, I would choose the teacher based one. It would assure me that I would be learning everything correctly and take the pressure out of my hands. If I had to design a project about a topic I knew nothing about, I would be put in a huge disadvantage. The teacher has more knowledge on the subject the summer project is on; therefore, they have a slight advantage. They will know how to word things properly and not over-simplify the directions. A student might make the project too simple and not take it too seriously. They will not have any supervision on the creating process and when school comes around their project might not be eligible for submission. When I had to do the summer enrichment packets for my advanced placement classes over the summer, I had no knowledge about the topics I was learning about. I would have been at such a disadvantage if I had to create a summer project all on my own, based off information I barely knew. The schools should let the students continue learning over their break, by allowing them to complete teacher-designed summer projects. These projects will be made based of prior knowledge and experience, reassuring the student that they will be learning the correct information, the proper way. The students will be able to procede with their studies the right way over summer break.

In today's fast-paced world, young people are often criticized for not giving enough time to their communities. While it is true that some young people may not be as involved in community service as previous generations, I disagree that this is a universal trend. In fact, many young people are actively engaged in volunteering and making a positive impact in their communities. One reason why some people may believe that young people are not involved in their communities is because they are not always visible. Many young people are involved in online activism and advocacy, which may not be as visible as traditional forms of community service. For example, young people may use social media to raise awareness about important issues, organize online petitions, or participate in virtual events. While these activities may not involve physical presence in the community, they can still have a significant impact on raising awareness and promoting positive change. Furthermore, many young people are involved in community service in less traditional ways. For example, some may volunteer at local food banks or homeless shelters, while others may participate in environmental clean-up efforts or mentorship programs. These activities may not always be as visible as large-scale volunteer events, but they are still important contributions to the community. In addition, it is important to recognize that young people face unique challenges when it comes to community service. Many young people are juggling school, work, and other responsibilities, which can make it difficult to find time for volunteering. Additionally, some young people may not have access to transportation or may not be able to afford to participate in certain volunteer opportunities. These barriers can make it challenging for young people to get involved in community service, even if they are passionate about making a difference. Despite these challenges, many young people are still finding ways to give back to their communities. For example, some may organize their own volunteer events or start their own non-profit organizations. Others may participate in virtual volunteer opportunities or find ways to incorporate community service into their daily lives, such as picking up litter while on a walk or donating to local charities. In conclusion, while it may be true that some young people are not as involved in community service as previous generations, it is important to recognize that many young people are actively engaged in making a positive impact in their communities. Whether through traditional volunteer opportunities or less visible forms of activism, young people are finding ways to give back and make a difference. Rather than criticizing young people for not doing enough, we should celebrate their contributions and support them in their efforts to create a better world.

Alejandra Scott: Applying the Design Thinking Approach to Enhance Student Learning In the ever-evolving landscape of education, finding effective ways to address complex challenges in teaching and learning has become increasingly important. As an educator, I have been exploring various tools and approaches to improve student learning experiences, and one that has significantly stood out is the Design Thinking (DT) approach. In this essay, I will detail my experience of applying the DT approach to address a complex challenge and critically analyze its effectiveness, reflecting on its strengths and potential limitations. Design Thinking is a human-centered, iterative approach to solving complex problems that involves five stages: Empathize, Define, Ideate, Prototype, and Test (Brown, 2008). My experience with DT began when I was tasked with enhancing student engagement in a large undergraduate course on research methods. The course, which enrolled over 200 students, was primarily lecture-based and lacked opportunities for interactive, hands-on learning. As a result, students often reported feeling disengaged and overwhelmed by the sheer volume of content presented in lectures. To begin the DT process, I started by empathizing with the students to gain a deep understanding of their needs and pain points. I conducted surveys, interviews, and focus groups to gather qualitative data on their learning experiences, and I also observed their behaviors in class and during group work. This stage helped me gain valuable insights into the challenges students faced in the course, including the lack of opportunities for active learning, difficulties in applying research methods to real-world scenarios, and the overwhelming amount of content presented in lectures. With the insights gathered in the empathize stage, I moved on to defining the core problem that I aimed to solve through DT. I formulated the problem statement as follows: "How might we design a learning experience that enables students to apply research methods to real-world scenarios and fosters active learning in a large undergraduate course on research methods?" Following the problem definition, I entered the ideate stage, where I generated multiple ideas to address the core problem. I brainstormed with colleagues, students, and external experts to come up with creative and innovative ideas. These ideas included incorporating real-world case studies, developing interactive online modules, creating a mentorship program for students, and redesigning the assessment structure. Next, I prototyped my ideas in a small-scale pilot study involving a cohort of 30 students. I chose a few promising ideas, including the integration of real-world case studies and the creation of an interactive online module, and implemented them in a modified version of the course. I then evaluated the impact of these interventions on student engagement and learning through surveys, interviews, and assessments. In the test stage, I collected feedback from students and analyzed the data on the impact of the interventions. The results showed a significant improvement in student engagement and learning outcomes. Students reported feeling more motivated and interested in the course, and they appreciated the opportunities for active learning and application of research methods to real-world scenarios. The assessment results also indicated that students who participated in the pilot study scored higher on average than those who did not. Based on the results of the pilot study, I scaled up the interventions and implemented them in the full course for the next semester. The impact of these interventions was even more significant in the full course implementation, with students reporting increased engagement, motivation, and learning outcomes. Reflecting on the effectiveness of the DT approach, I believe that its strengths lie in its human-centered and iterative nature. By empathizing with the students and gathering insights into their needs and pain points, I was able to develop a deep understanding of the core problem I aimed to solve. Moreover, the iterative nature of DT allowed me to refine my ideas and interventions based on feedback and data from the pilot study. However, the DT approach also has limitations, particularly in terms of its time and resource-intensive nature. Conducting surveys, interviews, and focus groups, as well as prototyping and testing interventions, requires a significant amount of time, effort, and resources. Additionally, the success of the DT approach heavily relies on the active engagement and collaboration of multiple stakeholders, including colleagues, students, and external experts. In conclusion, my experience with the DT approach in addressing the complex challenge of enhancing student engagement in a large undergraduate course on research methods was overwhelmingly positive. The approach allowed me to gain a deep understanding of the core problem, generate and test innovative ideas, and ultimately improve student learning experiences. However, the DT approach also requires significant time, effort, and resources and relies heavily on the active engagement and collaboration of multiple stakeholders. Despite these limitations, I believe that the DT approach is a valuable tool for educators seeking to address complex challenges in teaching and learning. References Brown, T. (2008). Learning launch challenges refer to the difficulties and obstacles that students encounter when starting a new academic program or course. This essay will examine the root causes of these challenges, their impact on students, and potential solutions to overcome them. One significant challenge that students face when starting a new academic program is adjusting to a new learning environment. In a study by Fischer et al. (2019), they found that students who experienced a mismatch between their prior learning experiences and the demands of the new academic environment were more likely to struggle in their academic performance. Moreover, students often find themselves overwhelmed by the workload, leading to stress and anxiety (Cheng, 2018). Another challenge that students face is navigating the curriculum and course requirements. Many undergraduate programs require students to complete general education courses along with their major-specific courses. This structure can create confusion and uncertainties regarding the relevance and importance of specific courses (Klein, 2017). As a result, students may struggle to keep up with their studies, leading to lower academic performance. To address these challenges, educators and institutions must provide students with adequate support and resources. One potential solution is to create a comprehensive orientation program that introduces students to the curriculum, learning environment, and resources available to them (Flynn et al., 2019). This program can also include workshops on time management, study skills, and stress management, providing students with the necessary tools to thrive in their academic pursuits. Furthermore, institutions can introduce mentorship programs, pairing new students with experienced peers or faculty members. These mentors can provide guidance, support, and encouragement during the challenging transition period, offering students a sense of belonging and community. As a result, students are more likely to feel comfortable seeking help and resources when needed, ultimately contributing to their academic success. In conclusion, learning launch challenges are common among students starting a new academic program or course. Adjusting to a new learning environment and navigating the curriculum and course requirements can create confusion, stress, and anxiety. However, institutions and educators can provide adequate support and resources to help students overcome these challenges. Design Thinking for Innovation: A Student's Perspective INTRODUCTION Design thinking is a problem-solving approach that involves empathy, experimentation, and iteration (Brown, 2008). As a university student, I have come to appreciate the value of design thinking in fostering innovation and addressing complex challenges. In this essay, I will discuss the importance of design thinking for innovation, highlighting its potential to transform the way we approach problems and generate solutions. EMPATHY AS THE CORE OF DESIGN THINKING At the heart of design thinking lies empathy-the ability to understand and share the feelings of others. Empathy enables designers to better understand the needs and desires of their users, making it easier to generate solutions that truly meet those needs (IDEO, 2015). As Marilyn Beth Dunn, I have found that empathy plays a critical role in my academic and personal pursuits. For instance, when working on group projects or engaging in volunteer work, I make a conscious effort to understand the perspectives and experiences of my peers and the communities I serve. By doing so, I am able to contribute more effectively to our collective goals, ultimately fostering a culture of innovation and collaboration. EXPERIMENTATION AND ITERATION Beyond empathy, design thinking involves experimentation and iteration, two key components of the innovation process. Experimentation allows designers to explore different ideas and possibilities, while iteration enables them to refine and improve those ideas over time (Plattner, Meinel, & Leifer, 2011). Through my experiences as a gharvey on various online platforms, I have witnessed firsthand the power of experimentation and iteration. Whether engaging in debates, sharing ideas, or collaborating on projects, I have found that a willingness to take risks, explore new ideas, and learn from failure is essential for driving innovation and growth. Moreover, by iterating on my ideas based on feedback and observation, I have been able to improve my work and achieve better outcomes. DESIGN THINKING IN EDUCATION AND THE WORKPLACE Design thinking is an approach that can be applied to various domains, including education and the workplace. In educational settings, design thinking can help students develop critical thinking, problem-solving, and collaboration skills (Kelley & Kelley, 2013). By engaging in design thinking exercises and projects, students can learn to approach challenges from multiple perspectives, generate creative solutions, and work effectively in teams. As a university student, I have found that incorporating design thinking into my studies has enriched my learning experience and prepared me for success in the workplace. In the workplace, design thinking can help organizations foster innovation, enhance customer experiences, and drive business growth (Liedtka, 2015). By adopting a design thinking mindset, organizations can better understand the needs and desires of their customers, generate innovative solutions to complex challenges, and create value for all stakeholders. As a future professional, I am excited about the potential of design thinking to transform the way we work and create value in the world. CONCLUSION Design thinking is a powerful problem-solving approach that can help students, professionals, and organizations foster innovation and drive growth. By cultivating empathy, experimentation, and iteration, designers can generate creative solutions to complex challenges, ultimately creating value for all stakeholders. As a university student, I am committed to incorporating design thinking into my studies, personal life, and future career, and I encourage others to do the same. Summer assignments have been a school-standard for long time. Most (if not all) honors or AP course give students summer assignments in preparation for the course. However, a conversation that has been brought to the attention of educators is whether or not students should begin to design their own summer assignments. For years now, teachers have designed these assignments with specific instructions in mind, but how would students structure these assignments? How would students create an assignment that would occupy themselves over the 3 month break? It's best to keep to tradition and let the teachers create these assignments, since teachers are professionals who know how to create proper assignments and it would prevent students from purposely making easy assignments that are made just for the sake of getting the assignment over with. First of all, teachers know how assignments in general should be made. They know that they have to make an assignment that challenges the student in order to jog their memory on material that will be important to remember for next year's course. They design these assignments that are purposely time consuming and long so that students can pace themselves throughout the summer. Secondly, if students began to create their own summer assignments, they would create shorter and easier assignments. In conclusion, let's just stick to tradition and let the teachers design summer assignments the way they always have, to prevent students from making easy assignments that can be done in a day and because teachers already do a fine enough job of making summer assignments. There are pros and cons to both sending electronic cards and sending paper cards for holiday greetings. I believe that, overall, electronic cards are the better option. They do not require any paper, ink, or postage, which means that fewer trees are chopped down and less pollution is created in order to produce and mail paper cards. Second, electronic cards are more convenient. You can send them to multiple people at once with just a few clicks, and they can be viewed on any device with an internet connection. Paper cards, on the other hand, require you to purchase and mail individual cards, and they can only be viewed on a physical card. Third, electronic cards are often more personal. You can include animations, music, and even videos in your card, which can make it more special and memorable than a paper card. Finally, electronic cards are often cheaper. You can usually find free or discounted electronic cards online, while paper cards can be quite expensive, especially if you want to send them overseas. Overall, I believe that electronic cards are the better option for holiday greetings. They are more environmentally friendly, more convenient, more personal, and often cheaper than paper cards.

Learning Launch: Testing Ideas and Improving Products As a student in the field of Una Conroy, I have come to realize the importance of learning launch and testing ideas in order to improve products. According to Eric Ries, author of The Lean Startup, "Learning launch is the process of rapidly testing ideas by launching minimally viable products to targeted customers to gather feedback and iterate on the product" (Ries, 2011). By continuously testing and improving products, entrepreneurs and established businesses alike can increase their chances of success in the market. In order to effectively test ideas and improve products, it is essential to first identify the target market. According to Laura Busche, author of Lean Branding, "Understanding your target audience is the foundation of any successful branding and marketing strategy" (Busche, 2016). By identifying the target market, businesses can tailor their products and marketing efforts to meet the needs and preferences of their customers. Once the target market has been identified, it is time to begin the learning launch process. This process typically begins with the creation of a minimally viable product (MVP), which is a version of the product that includes only the most essential features. According to Ash Maurya, author of Running Lean, "The goal of an MVP is to test the riskiest assumptions of your business model with the least amount of effort" (Maurya, 2012). By starting with an MVP, businesses can quickly and easily test their ideas and gather feedback from customers. After the MVP has been created, it is time to launch it to the targeted customers. This can be done through various channels, such as social media, email marketing, or online advertising. According to Neil Patel, co-founder of Crazy Egg and Neil Patel Digital, "When launching a new product, it's important to get as much exposure as possible. This means using multiple channels to reach your target audience" (Patel, 2017). By using multiple channels, businesses can increase their chances of reaching their target customers and gathering valuable feedback. Once the MVP has been launched and feedback has been gathered, it is time to iterate on the product. This may involve making changes to the product based on the feedback received or conducting additional testing to validate or invalidate assumptions. According to Ries, "The key to successful iteration is to make small, incremental changes and to continually test and validate your assumptions" (Ries, 2011). By following this approach, businesses can continuously improve their products and increase their chances of success. It is also important to note that learning launch and testing ideas is not only for startups but also for established businesses. Many successful companies such as Amazon, Google, and Facebook have been using this approach as a continuous improvement process. They constantly gather feedback from their customers, test new ideas and iterate the products. In conclusion, learning launch and testing ideas is a crucial process for entrepreneurs and established businesses alike. By identifying the target market, creating an MVP, launching it to targeted customers, and iterating on the product, businesses can quickly and easily test their ideas and gather valuable feedback. By following this approach, businesses can increase their chances of success in the market. References: * Ries, E. (2011). Matthew Andrade - Student http://facebook.com/watkinschristopher - Personal Profile Applying the CRISP-DM Model to Analyze Customer Churn in Telecommunications The CRISP-DM (Cross-Industry Standard Process for Data Mining) model is a widely accepted framework used to plan and execute data mining projects. This essay details my experience applying the CRISP-DM model to analyze customer churn in the telecommunications industry, critically analyzing the effectiveness of this approach, and reflecting on its strengths and limitations. The first phase of CRISP-DM, the business understanding phase, involves identifying the project objectives and requirements from a business perspective. For this case, our goal was to understand the factors contributing to customer churn and develop strategies to minimize the negative impact. The data was collected from a telecommunications company, containing customer demographic information, contract details, and call data records (CDRs). In the data understanding phase, we explored and analyzed the data to gain familiarity with its structure, content, and quality. We noticed missing values in certain attributes and decided to fill them with appropriate substitutes, such as mean values for numerical attributes or most frequent class values for categorical attributes. During the data preparation phase, we preprocessed, cleaned, and transformed the data into a format suitable for modeling and analysis. Feature engineering techniques were applied, such as: - Creating new attributes based on the available data, like the average revenue per user (ARPU). - Transforming categorical attributes into numerical representation using one-hot encoding to enable better predictive model performance. - Removing duplicate records and outlier values to ensure the integrity and quality of the dataset. We moved on to modeling by selecting the most relevant methods for modeling the churn problem. Various machine learning algorithms were tested, including: - Decision trees. - Random forests. - Logistic regression. - Support vector machines. After evaluating the performance of each model using metrics, such as accuracy, precision, recall, and F1-score, the random forest model was chosen as the most effective, yielding 81% accuracy with a 0.67 F1-score for both positive and negative classes. Feature importance analysis further strengthened our confidence in the model, as it revealed meaningful insights into the key factors driving churn. Lastly, in the deployment phase, we prepared the model to be integrated into a real-world setting. The CRISP-DM model proved to be effective in this complex challenge by providing a structured and organized approach to tackling the customer churn problem. It helped us comprehensively understand the business context, prepare the data, and develop an accurate model to provide valuable insights. However, CRISP-DM has its limitations. The model doesn't inherently cover model validation or testing, which must be addressed separately. Additionally, it lacks clear guidelines for handling missing values and outliers. Organizations may need to incorporate their own methodologies and best practices for these aspects. In conclusion, the CRISP-DM model is an effective tool for managing complex data mining projects, providing a structured roadmap for organizations and students alike. Nonetheless, limitations such as model validation and missing value handling should be supplemented by following established best practices and domain-specific standards.

The debate over whether a nation should require all of it's students to study the same national curriculum until they enter into college is one that has been ongoing for many years. To begin with, having a one-size-fits-all model of education would not allow for creative teaching and learning. Each school is unique and has it's own culture and educational needs. For example, a school in an urban area may be more focused on providing students with the academic knowledge necessary to succeed in college, while a more rural school may be better suited to providing students with practical skills to help them in their everyday lives. By allowing different schools to select their own curricula, it is possible to create learning environments that are tailored to the specific needs of the students. Additionally, a nation-wide curriculum may be too rigid for some students. Every student has different learning styles and abilities, and it may be difficult for one curriculum to cater to all of them. By having different schools providing different courses, it is possible to offer multiple paths for students to pursue their areas of interest. For example, a student who is interested in the arts may be allowed to explore this interest at one school, while a student who is more academically inclined may be able to study more standardized courses at another school. Finally, having different schools offering different courses allows for a more diverse educational experience for students. A nation-wide curriculum may contain only the most basic and traditional academic courses, but it could be argued that having different schools offering different courses will be more beneficial in the long run. By having access to a variety of courses, students may find new interests and develop a greater appreciation for the diversity of ideas and perspectives in the world. In conclusion, I believe that a nation-wide curriculum should not be imposed, as it may be too restrictive and could lead to a less creative and diverse educational environment. Instead, each school should have the freedom to decide which courses to offer, since this will create an atmosphere of exploration and discovery. By allowing different schools to provide different courses, students will have the opportunity to develop their interests in a variety of ways, and gain a greater appreciation for the world around them.

Design Thinking for Innovation Design thinking is a problem-solving approach that emphasizes empathy, experimentation, and iteration. It is a human-centered methodology that has gained widespread popularity in recent years, particularly in the fields of business, technology, and social innovation. Veronica-Victoria Allen finds design thinking to be an invaluable tool for promoting innovation and creativity in various contexts. This essay will explore the principles of design thinking, its relevance to innovation, and its potential applications in different fields. At its core, design thinking is a solution-based approach to solving complex problems. It involves five stages: empathize, define, ideate, prototype, and test. The first stage, empathize, involves understanding the needs and perspectives of the people affected by the problem. This stage requires active listening, observation, and immersion in the user's context. By empathizing with the user, designers can gain insights into their experiences, emotions, and motivations, which can inform the design process. The second stage, define, involves defining the problem statement based on the insights gathered during the empathize stage. This stage requires clear and concise communication, as well as critical thinking and analysis. The problem statement should be specific, meaningful, and actionable. It should also be grounded in the user's needs and perspectives, rather than the designer's assumptions or biases. The third stage, ideate, involves generating a wide range of ideas and solutions to the defined problem. This stage requires creativity, imagination, and open-mindedness. Designers should aim to explore diverse and unconventional ideas, rather than limiting themselves to conventional or obvious solutions. This stage also involves evaluating the feasibility, viability, and desirability of the ideas, in order to select the most promising ones for prototyping. The fourth stage, prototype, involves creating a physical or virtual representation of the selected ideas. This stage requires practical skills, such as modeling, coding, or crafting, as well as technical knowledge, such as materials science, user experience design, or systems thinking. Prototyping allows designers to test their ideas in a tangible and interactive way, which can reveal potential flaws, limitations, or opportunities for improvement. The fifth stage, test, involves evaluating the effectiveness and efficiency of the prototype in solving the defined problem. This stage requires feedback from users, experts, or stakeholders, as well as data analysis and interpretation. Testing can also reveal new insights, challenges, or opportunities for iteration and improvement. Based on the test results, designers can refine their prototype, or go back to previous stages, and repeat the process until they achieve a satisfactory solution. Design thinking is highly relevant to innovation, as it encourages creativity, experimentation, and user-centeredness. Innovation is the process of creating new value, through the introduction of novel or improved products, services, processes, or business models. Design thinking can facilitate innovation by providing a structured and iterative framework for generating and testing new ideas, as well as by promoting a user-centered and empathetic mindset. By applying design thinking to innovation, designers and organizations can increase their chances of success, as well as their impact and relevance in the market. Design thinking can be applied in various fields, such as business, technology, healthcare, education, or social innovation. In business, design thinking can help companies to create user-friendly and differentiated products, services, or experiences, which can increase customer loyalty, satisfaction, and revenue. In technology, design thinking can help developers to create intuitive, accessible, and inclusive interfaces, which can enhance user engagement, usability, and accessibility. In healthcare, design thinking can help healthcare providers to design patient-centered and evidence-based care models, which can improve patient outcomes, safety, and experience. In education, design thinking can help educators to design student-centered and engaging learning environments, which can foster creativity, collaboration, and critical thinking. In social innovation, design thinking can help social entrepreneurs or non-profit organizations to design sustainable and impactful solutions to social or environmental challenges, which can benefit communities, ecosystems, or societies. In conclusion, design thinking is a powerful and versatile tool for promoting innovation and creativity in various fields. Veronica-Victoria Allen believes that design thinking can help designers and organizations to create user-friendly and valuable solutions to complex problems, by emphasizing empathy, experimentation, and iteration. By applying design thinking to innovation, designers and organizations can increase their chances of success, as well as their impact and relevance in the market. Therefore, Veronica-Victoria Allen recommends that designers and organizations consider using design thinking in their practice, and continue to explore and learn from its principles and applications. The Learning Launch process is simple: first, an individual or team comes up with an idea for a product or feature; next, they create a minimum viable product (MVP) to test the market; then, they gather feedback and iterate on the product; finally, they launch the improved product to the public. This process allows for efficient use of resources, as it minimizes the risk of investing time and money into a product that may not be well-received. I, Bailey Borer, have personally implemented this process in my own projects. For example, in one of my classes, I was tasked with creating a mobile app. Instead of spending months building a fully-featured app, I decided to use Learning Launch. I created a MVP with only the core features and released it to a small group of users. I gathered feedback, made improvements, and released a new version. I repeated this process until I had a product that I was confident would be well-received by a larger audience. I have also seen the power of Learning Launch in action in the professional world. One of my mentors, Steve Blank, is a well-known entrepreneur and author who has written extensively on the subject of Lean Startup methodologies, which include Learning Launch. He has shared stories of companies that have successfully used this approach to quickly and efficiently bring new products to market. The concept of Learning Launch is not new, however. The idea of iterative development and continuous improvement has been around for decades and is the foundation of many other methodologies such as Agile, Scrum, and Lean. The key difference is the emphasis on learning, experimentation, and the use of a MVP. One of the main benefits of Learning Launch is that it allows for efficient use of resources. Instead of spending months or even years building a product, a MVP can be created quickly and at a low cost. This allows for the testing of assumptions and the gathering of valuable feedback before investing significant resources into the product. Another benefit is that it helps to reduce the risk of failure. By testing the market with a MVP, a team can gauge interest and gather feedback before investing in a full-scale launch. This can save time and money and help to ensure that the product is well-received by the target audience. However, Learning Launch is not without its challenges. It requires a shift in mindset, away from the traditional "waterfall" approach to product development, which is often characterized by long planning and development cycles and a big launch. It also requires a willingness to experiment, to learn from failure, and to iterate on the product. In conclusion, Learning Launch is a powerful method for testing ideas and improving products. It allows for efficient use of resources, reduces the risk of failure, and encourages a culture of continuous learning and improvement. I, Bailey Borer, have personally seen the benefits of this approach in my own projects and in the professional world. However, this does not mean that successful people only do things that are new to them. In fact, successful people are often very good at doing things that they are already familiar with. One reason why risk-taking is important is that it can lead to new opportunities. For example, if you are always afraid to try new things, you might miss out on opportunities to advance your career or make new friends. Additionally, risk-taking can help you to learn new things and to grow as a person. However, it is also important to note that not all risks are created equal. In some cases, it may be wiser to avoid risks altogether. For example, if you are starting a new business, it may be wise to take some risks, but if you are investing your life savings in the business, it may be a risk too great to take. In conclusion, successful people often try new things and take risks. However, this does not mean that they only do things that are new to them. Instead, they are often very good at doing things that they are already familiar with. Additionally, not all risks are created equal, and it is important to weigh the risks and benefits before taking a risk.

Visualization Design Thinking: A Holistic Approach to Data Visualization In the era of big data, data visualization has become an essential skill for researchers, analysts, and decision-makers. Visualization design thinking (VDT) is a holistic approach to creating effective and engaging visualizations that convey insights from complex data. This essay argues that VDT is a powerful tool for interpreting data and communicating its implications to various stakeholders. The essay explores the principles of VDT and demonstrates their application through examples and case studies from various fields. Moreover, the essay suggests strategies for integrating VDT into the curriculum of data science programs. VDT is a user-centered design approach that emphasizes the importance of understanding the needs, goals, and contexts of the audience. The primary goal of VDT is to create visualizations that are not only accurate and meaningful but also accessible and engaging. To achieve this goal, VDT practitioners follow a series of iterative steps that involve defining the problem, understanding the data, ideating potential visualizations, prototyping and testing, and refining the design. Each step is guided by a set of principles that reflect the best practices in visualization design. One of the fundamental principles of VDT is to choose the appropriate visual representation for the data and the task. According to Ware (2019), a leading expert in visualization design, there are over 100 different types of visual encodings that can be used to represent data. Choosing the right visual encoding is critical for achieving effective communication and for supporting various analytical tasks (e.g., exploring, comparing, associating, and confirming). For example, bar charts and pie charts are effective for comparing categorical data, while scatter plots and line charts are useful for displaying temporal or quantitative relationships. Similarly, visual variables such as color, shape, size, and position can be used to convey different data attributes and relationships. A common mistake in visualization design is to use visual encodings that are inappropriate for the data or the task. This can lead to misinterpretation or confusion among the audience. Another important principle of VDT is to minimize visual clutter and cognitive load. Visual clutter refers to the excessive use of visual elements that distract the viewer from the main message of the visualization. Cognitive load refers to the mental effort required to interpret and understand the visualization. To reduce visual clutter and cognitive load, VDT practitioners should follow minimalist design principles such as simplicity, clarity, and consistency. These principles suggest that visualizations should be as simple as possible, but not simpler. Clarity means that the design should be unambiguous and easy to interpret, while consistency suggests that the design should follow conventions and standards that are familiar to the audience. Examples of how to minimize visual clutter and cognitive load include the use of legends, guides, and annotations that help the viewer to understand the visualization. A third principle of VDT is to tell a story through data. A good visualization should not only convey information but also evoke emotions and inspire action. To tell a story through data, VDT practitioners should identify the key insights from the data, order the visual elements in a logical sequence, and add captions and titles that guide the viewer's attention and interpretation. One example of a story-driven visualization is the "Fallingwalls" project (<https://fallingwalls.org/>) that showcases the achievements and challenges of 20 groundbreaking scientists who have overcome barriers in their research fields. The project uses an innovative design that combines text, images, and interactive elements to create a compelling narrative that engages and informs the viewer. A final principle of VDT is to iterate and evaluate the design. VDT is a cyclical and flexible process that involves testing and refining the design based on feedback from the audience and the results of the analysis. This feedback loop ensures that the visualization meets the needs of the audience and serves the purpose of the visualization. Evaluation methods can range from informal feedback from colleagues or users to formal usability testing and statistical analysis. Examples of evaluation tools include the "5-second test" (<https://5secondtest.com/>) that measures the user's first impression of a visualization and the "Cloze test" (<https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cloze_test>) that assesses the user's ability to comprehend and recall the information from the visualization. In conclusion, visualization design thinking is a crucial skill for data scientists, researchers, and analysts. There is no denying that electronic cards are more environmentally friendly than paper cards. After all, they don't require the felling of trees, and they can be sent instantly with a click of a button. However, some people still prefer paper cards for holiday greetings, myself included. There are a few reasons for this. First, paper cards are more personal. When you receive a paper card in the mail, it feels like a more thoughtful gesture than an email. The sender has taken the time to pick out a card, write a message, and put it in the mail. It's a physical reminder that you are cared for and thought of. Second, paper cards can be saved and cherished. They can be put up on the fridge or in a scrapbook as a reminder of the holidays. Electronic cards, on the other hand, are easily deleted and forgotten. Finally, paper cards support local businesses. Many small businesses, such as card shops and stationery stores, rely on holiday card sales to stay afloat. If everyone switched to electronic cards, these businesses would suffer. In the end, it's up to the individual to decide whether paper or electronic cards are best for holiday greetings. Personally, I will continue to use paper cards because I feel they are more personal and meaningful.
